title: Displaced persons
hook: survivors wait in camps for somewhere to go

segments.voice: Yesterday, your line: two memories of one year. Did you listen for the memory you hear less often? Today we step back a little in time, to the survivors who were still waiting for a place. Day one thousand twenty-six.

A camp in Germany, after the war. Wooden barracks, sometimes old army buildings, sometimes the same kind of fences. But today there's a wedding in one of the halls. The bride's dress, the story goes, was sewn from parachute silk. Someone has found a fiddle. Someone has baked something that is almost a cake. Outside, the same barracks, the same fence, the same waiting. Inside, people dance. Today's word is the plain official name for the people in that hall.
screen: `A WEDDING IN THE BARRACKS.` → `A DRESS OF PARACHUTE SILK.` → `INSIDE, PEOPLE DANCE.`

segments.voice: The Allies had a bureaucratic term for people the war had torn from home: displaced persons. DPs, for short. Jewish survivors who could not or would not go back ended up in DP camps in Germany, Austria and Italy. Why not just go home? Because home was gone. Families had been murdered. Houses and shops had been taken by others. And in some towns, survivors who returned were met with hostility, and even with violence. So people came back to the camps, or never left them. Meanwhile, other doors opened slowly, when they opened at all. The British, who then ruled Palestine, held Jewish immigration under tight limits, and ships carrying survivors there were stopped at sea. So the survivors waited. And waiting, they lived. They called themselves by a Hebrew name, She'erit Hapletah: the surviving remnant. They opened schools and printed newspapers. They staged plays, held elections, trained to farm. They married, and babies were born in the barracks. The prophet Jeremiah once wrote a letter to exiles in Babylon, people waiting far from home, and told them not to put their lives on hold: "Build ye houses, and dwell in them." Plant gardens, he wrote. Marry. Raise children where you are. The survivors in the camps did something like that. They had a roof, and food, and each other. What they didn't have was a place that was theirs. Nowhere to go is not the same as nothing to do. They built a life in the waiting room.
screen: `DISPLACED PERSONS: DPS.` · `HOME WAS GONE; SHIPS STOPPED AT SEA.` · `THE SURVIVING REMNANT.` · then, large: `BUILD YE HOUSES, AND DWELL IN THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of people with nowhere to go. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind people who are waiting right now for somewhere to go: in camps, at borders, in shelters, sleeping in cars. You don't need to know their names. Picture one ordinary detail. A bag packed and repacked. A child doing homework on a cot. A phone charging in a hallway. Stay with that one detail. If you pray, you can pray for people waiting for a place. If you don't, hold them in mind with care. The bell holds the time.
Displaced persons. The official name for people the war tore from home. For Jewish survivors, it meant long waits in camps for somewhere to go. Today's word.
Your line: nowhere to go. Today, give something, time, money or a kind word, to someone who is far from home. Day one thousand twenty-six.

howItsDone: Some Jewish families keep photographs and documents from the DP camps where their parents or grandparents waited, and Jewish organizations that once aided DPs still work with refugees today.

notes: Audit: the teach had five screen heads (the guide asks for 3-4 for the order game); 'why not go home?' and 'ships stopped at sea' merged into one head. Jeremiah 29:5 JPS 1917 wording checked ('Build ye houses, and dwell in them'). Note the Jeremiah parallel is loose by design: DP survivors mostly sought to leave Germany, not settle there; the script says only 'something like that'.

Claims rule: no counts of DPs, camps or births; the camp locations (Germany, Austria, Italy) are general, please check. Postwar violence against returning survivors (e.g. Kielce) is unnamed and undated.
Parachute-silk wedding dress is attributed ('the story goes'); one such dress is held by the US Holocaust Memorial Museum.
British limits on Jewish immigration and turned-back ships (e.g. the Exodus) are stated without names or dates; please check.
She'erit Hapletah: the phrase has biblical echoes (e.g. 1 Chronicles 4:43, Ezra 9:14); the script gives no etymology. Please check the original-game vocalization.
Note on order: this day steps back to 1945–48 after day 1025's 1948; the review says so.

Editor: Exodus 23:9 ('ye know the heart of a stranger... strangers in the land of Egypt') repeated day 1010's Deuteronomy 10:19 and its closed-doors angle; replaced with Jeremiah 29:5–6 (the letter to the exiles: build houses, plant gardens, marry), which fits the life built while waiting. Please confirm the JPS 1917 wording of the quoted half-verse. 'Closed doors, turned-back ships' became 'ships stopped at sea' (many intercepted passengers were held in camps rather than sent back), and the hook's line at a board of names (day 1019's lists) was replaced. The Exodus 23:9 note above no longer applies.
